title: Robots & Self-Driving Cars
hook: When AI leaves the screen and gets a body, the rules change. The physical world is messy and unforgiving — which is why self-driving cars and helpful robots arrived slower than promised.
key_points: 'Embodied AI' acts in the real world — cars, delivery bots, warehouse and home robots.
The physical world is far harder than text: rare events, split-second stakes, no undo.
Self-driving exists but rolled out slowly and cautiously; full autonomy is still partial.
Real questions: safety, liability when it goes wrong, and effects on driving jobs.
content_html: Most AI you meet lives on a screen. But a major frontier is embodied AI — putting that intelligence into machines that move through and act on the physical world: self-driving cars, sidewalk delivery bots, warehouse robots, and the long-promised helpful robot around the house. It's a natural next step, and progress is real. Yet anyone who remembers being told fully self-driving cars were "two years away" — for many years running — has learned the key lesson: the physical world is brutally harder than text.
extra_html: Here's why. A chatbot that says something wrong wastes a moment, and you just try again. A two-ton car that does something wrong at speed can kill someone — there's no undo, no second draft, and the stakes are immediate. The real world is also endlessly messy and full of rare, weird situations ("edge cases"): a couch in the road, a cyclist doing something unexpected, snow covering the lane lines, a police officer waving you through a red light. Humans handle these with common sense; AI, which has no real understanding, can be brittle exactly when it matters most. That's why self-driving has rolled out cautiously and unevenly — impressive robotaxis operating in limited, mapped areas, and "driver assist" features that still legally require a human ready to take over, rather than true go-anywhere autonomy. The same goes for robots: great in the controlled environment of a warehouse, still clumsy in the chaos of a home. And the hardest questions aren't even technical — who's liable when an autonomous machine causes harm, how safe is safe enough to deploy, and what happens to the millions of people who drive for a living? Embodied AI is coming, but the gap between a clever demo and a machine you'd trust with your life on a highway is exactly the gap this technology is still working to close.

related.title: AI Agents: AI That Does Things
related.hook: A chatbot answers; an agent acts. The new frontier is AI that can browse, click, book, and complete multi-step tasks for you — powerful, and exactly why you keep it on a leash.

related.title: AI & Jobs
related.hook: AI is less likely to take your whole job than to take certain tasks within it. The pattern through history: tools reshape work faster than they erase it.

related.title: What AI Can't Do
related.hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.

related.title: When the Drone Decides: AI and Autonomous Weapons
related.hook: Ukraine reportedly ran a one-time test of fully autonomous drones that chose and struck targets with no human pulling the trigger. The 'killer robot' debate just stopped being hypothetical.
